video_title: 278: Paul Kedrosky, Managing Partner, SK Ventures
gist: Paul Kedrosky (SK Ventures, MIT) argues the AI capex boom is a uniquely fragile bubble because it combines all four historical bubble pillars (technology, real estate, credit, government), with Nvidia acting as the 'central bank of AI' and neo-clouds and Oracle as debt-laden recipients of fragility. He sees a de facto tightening cycle (Texas go-slow policy, Nvidia leadership change), overestimated TAM from hyper-deflating tokens and a software-engineer early-adopter cohort, a Koo-style rate-insensitive deleveraging ahead, and a tail risk of white-collar labor itself being repriced.

themes.theme: Four-pillar bubble framework: tech, real estate, credit, government

insights.claim: Kedrosky argues the biggest manias in Western economic history (South Sea Bubble, railroads, canals, rural electrification, fiber, the GFC) each rested on one or more of four pillars: a technology story, loose credit, real estate, and active government encouragement.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Use the four-pillar checklist to gauge how systemic a boom is; more pillars present means more fragility.

insights.claim: The current AI build-out is unusual because it combines all four pillars at comparable strength: AI as the technology, loose credit, data centers treated as commercial real estate yield instruments, and a US government that sees AI as an existential race with China.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Kedrosky sees this as an 'almost irrational bubble'; size systemic tail hedges accordingly rather than treating AI risk as a single-sector bet.
insights.quote: Data centers become like apartment buildings full of GPUs

insights.claim: Executive orders over the past two and a half years, including EPA changes allowing broader sulfur dioxide emissions for behind-the-meter natural gas turbines that avoid grid interconnection, have created a cumulative policy tailwind accelerating the AI build-out.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Government support acts like a put under AI capex; watch for policy reversals as a key unwind trigger.

insights.claim: Participants in each silo (powered-land real estate investors, GPU technology investors, lenders) each view their own activity as rational, but the confluence of their discrete activities across the economy is what creates systemic fragility.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Fragility is emergent and invisible from within any one asset class; cross-asset monitoring is required.

insights.claim: The GFC sat at the intersection of real estate, government policy and credit without a strong technology story, while the fiber bubble combined technology and credit without real estate; railroads had all four.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Railroads, not dot-com or GFC, are the closest full-pillar historical analog for the AI build-out.

themes.theme: Private-market froth and a Koo-style balance-sheet deleveraging

insights.claim: The combined private-market valuations of SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI are roughly equivalent in nominal terms to the peak valuation of the Nasdaq at the top of the dot-com bubble.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Equity froth has migrated to private markets; IPOs like Anthropic's transfer that valuation risk to public investors.
insights.quote: SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI in nominal terms, the valuations in the private markets of those three firms are roughly equivalent to the peak valuation of the Nasdaq at the peak of the dot-com bubble.

insights.claim: Kedrosky contends the dot-com bust was compartmentalized within equity markets, whereas the GFC was a credit problem driven by shadow banking and misleading credit ratings; the AI moment contains elements of both.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Expect both equity drawdowns and credit contagion channels if the AI cycle turns.

insights.claim: The best analog for the aftermath of the AI capex boom is Richard Koo's balance-sheet recession (Japan after its 1980s-90s real estate boom): hyperscalers that entered with pristine balance sheets are leveraging up and will face a prolonged deleveraging largely insensitive to falling interest rates.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Don't count on rate cuts to revive capex after the peak; position for a long, rate-insensitive capex downturn.
insights.quote: what we will see on the other side of this is a prolonged deleveraging that will be largely insensitive to interest rate declines because they are deleveraging

insights.claim: In the GFC, leverage such as Merrill Lynch at 35-to-one stayed warehoused on bank balance sheets, whereas today much AI-related debt is being moved around the system.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host) / Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Debt dispersion makes it harder to locate where AI credit losses will land.

themes.theme: Overbuild as feature: tech works, investors pay

insights.claim: Believing AI is a transformative technology and believing its financing is a bubble are not contradictory; electrification, autos and railroads were consequential technologies that still produced financial crashes such as 1929 and repeated Erie Railroad collapses.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Separate the technology call from the investment-return call; the tech can win while capital is destroyed.

insights.claim: Kedrosky calls AI probably among the most important IT technologies of the last 100 years, and argues that this importance is precisely what lets it attract such enormous capex.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The strength of the narrative is the fuel for the overbuild, not a reason to dismiss bubble risk.

insights.claim: Like canal, railroad, electricity, office-automation and fiber build-outs, AI capex shows a growing share of non-residential fixed investment, a rising contribution to GDP growth, and leakage into other markets, including AI fundraising pressuring Treasury markets at the margin in late summer.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Watch AI debt issuance as a source of rates-market pressure and crowding out.

insights.claim: Zuckerberg has framed the risk of moving too slowly on AI as greater than the risk of overspending, accepting capital burn to avoid being left behind.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capex is driven by competitive fear rather than ROI discipline, raising overbuild risk.

insights.claim: Unlike prior episodes, today's participants explicitly justify overspending by citing Carlota Perez's thesis that overbuild cycles always work out; using historical description as ex-ante justification adds a feedback loop that accelerates both the build-out and its eventual failures.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: When 'it always works out' becomes the alibi, discount management capex rationales more heavily.
insights.quote: People weren't telling themselves when they built the railroads that overbuilding railroads always works out, right?

themes.theme: Token hyperdeflation and the TAM extrapolation error

insights.claim: Kedrosky describes AI tokens as the first hyper-deflationary industrial commodity, deflating by some measures about 13-fold year over year, which implies token volume must double roughly every 95 days just for revenue to stand still.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Track token volume growth versus price declines; any slowdown in volume below a ~95-day doubling implies shrinking revenue.
insights.quote: That implies that roughly every 95 days the volume of tokens must double just to stand still.

insights.claim: The industry implicitly assumes infinite price elasticity of demand for tokens, extrapolating three or four years of data, but demand is bounded, so interlocking growth and price-collapse exponentials make overbuild and fragility more severe.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of Jevons-style demand arguments used to justify capex; elasticity will flatten.
insights.quote: I do not want 100 cars if the price of cars drops to zero.

insights.claim: Ramp's spending data shows venture-backed companies are by far the largest per-employee spenders on AI, by something like 99 to 1, meaning AI demand depends heavily on unprofitable, VC-funded firms.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: AI revenue is exposed to VC funding conditions; a venture downturn would hit AI vendor revenue directly.

insights.claim: Early leaks from Anthropic's S-1 showed that about a year ago Meta was roughly 18% of Anthropic's revenue, illustrating heavy customer concentration in the software industry.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Scrutinize customer concentration in frontier-lab filings; loss of one big buyer is material.

insights.claim: AI adoption is concentrated in software engineers because code provides a ground-truth signal (it works or it doesn't) that enables autonomous, token-heavy iteration, whereas memos, emails and slide decks lack that signal and degrade with unsupervised iterations.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Token-intensive agentic usage may not generalize to the broader white-collar market; model demand curves accordingly.
insights.quote: Can I let a model loose on a memo and have it get better over the next 12 hours? It will get uniformly worse.

insights.claim: Naive extrapolation from this unusual early-adopter cohort leads to a huge overestimation of AI's total addressable market, violating the venture-capital tenet of never extrapolating your eventual market from your earliest buyers.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Haircut AI TAM and revenue forecasts built on coding-tool adoption curves.

themes.theme: Sources and destinations of fragility: Oracle, neo-clouds, Nvidia as central bank

insights.claim: Oracle is a 'destination of fragility': it is using prodigious debt to escape a mature, declining database business via AI, teetering near another ratings downgrade, with its CDS and bond spreads trading accordingly.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Oracle CDS and spreads are a key stress gauge; a downgrade could be an early contagion event.

insights.claim: Many neo-clouds pivoted from unprofitable crypto mining to AI compute, using vast amounts of debt to build out GPU farms, making them recipients of fragility.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Neo-cloud credit is among the most vulnerable links; watch their CDS and refinancing.

insights.claim: Kedrosky calls Nvidia the 'central bank of AI', running a quasi-fractional reserve system through unsecured lending and repayment schedules stretched into the future without cash exchange, effectively creating a currency akin to a shadow banking system.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Nvidia's vendor financing is the system's liquidity source; any tightening there propagates to its customers.
insights.quote: I often call Nvidia the central bank of AI

insights.claim: Pressure on Nvidia to keep growing revenue led Jensen Huang to stretch export rules, with GPUs servicing China via Southeast Asian cloud services, transshipment or black-market chips.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Export-control enforcement is a revenue and governance risk for Nvidia.

insights.claim: Frontier AI labs sit awkwardly in the middle of the system, neither true cloud providers nor able to stand without them, and Kedrosky does not hold much hope for them over time.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Be cautious on frontier-lab equity, including IPOs, given structural dependence on cloud providers.

insights.claim: Nvidia's summer plan to backstop GPU prices with a roughly $500 billion facility reportedly involving Blackstone and Goldman was effectively an attempted currency peg that the market saw as insufficiently backed and that never fully materialized.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host) / Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: GPUs function as currency in AI; attempts to peg their value signal stress and invite a 'break the peg' moment.
insights.quote: This was an attempt at a currency peg, right?

themes.theme: De facto AI tightening cycle: Texas, midterms, Nvidia leadership change

insights.claim: By AI data center build-out, the largest 'sovereign' is the US excluding Texas, second is China, and third is Texas, whose governor-elect has announced a go-slow policy on data centers after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: State-level policy shifts in Texas are a major swing factor for data center capex and power demand.
insights.quote: The third largest in the world is Texas.

insights.claim: Kedrosky argues the post-midterm period is a clear tightening moment for AI that the market initially misread as positive before selling off; the bull argument that fewer data centers protects margins is faith-based since inference capacity can be built in China or elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Treat restrictive data center policy as negative for AI capex names, not margin-protective.
insights.quote: you no longer have an empirical argument, you have a theological argument

insights.claim: With Nvidia moving to an interim CEO, its earnings call signaled more caution on lending to neo-clouds, which account for something on the order of 60% of token sales, meaning neo-clouds have entered a credit tightening cycle.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Reduced Nvidia vendor financing raises neo-cloud funding costs and default risk; CoreWeave CDS is a tell.
insights.quote: Neo Clouds just found out that they're they just entered a tightening cycle.

themes.theme: Misleading indicators and the true tail risk: repricing white-collar labor

insights.claim: GPU rental price indices (e.g., from Bloomberg) are close to useless as AI health indicators because they average across very dispersed providers and conflate tight-supply spot buyers with hyperscaler long-term contract pricing, a Simpson's-paradox problem.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Don't take flat or rising GPU rental prices (as cited by Jensen Huang) as evidence the AI cycle is healthy.

insights.claim: Nvidia has repeatedly protected margins through engineered scarcity: first in premium gaming after losing the mainstream graphics market to consoles, then in crypto (gross margins around 55-60%), and again with generative AI after crypto fell off in 2022.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Current GPU pricing reflects deliberate scarcity, so margins may compress once scarcity can't be maintained.

insights.claim: Kedrosky's 'out there' tail risk: AI providers justify capex by targeting a material share of global white-collar labor (around $5 trillion of revenue by 2031-32), but capturing a slice of a commodity reprices the whole market, shrinking the white-collar labor pool itself.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The bigger systemic risk may be labor income and tax-base erosion, not CDS or token prices.
insights.quote: You don't reprice the corner of a commodity. You reprice the entire thing.

insights.claim: Repricing of white-collar labor in aging societies with high dependency ratios could leave households and the social funding system, not banks or AI firms, as the entity needing a bailout.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Consider sovereign fiscal and consumer credit exposure as second-order AI tail risks.

insights.claim: Kedrosky calls the rapid expansion of AI-enabled cyberattacks 'the hackening': about 8% of all critical software vulnerabilities ever found were found in the first three weeks of October this year, and 50% since January.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Expect elevated systemic cyber incidents (airlines, banks, gas supply); cyber defense spend and insurance repricing follow.
insights.quote: 50% of all the critical software vulnerabilities in installed software were found since January of this year.

insights.claim: Unlike the lean-vol pre-GFC period when bank CDS traded at 20-25 basis points, the current cycle shows high but largely uncorrelated single-stock volatility in equities.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: Dispersion is high; tail hedges are not as cheap as pre-GFC, so pick specific stress points.

insights.claim: Kedrosky frames early-stage venture as buying long-dated call options in illiquid markets, and only invests when a company has a plausible mechanism to go 'explosively right' and the option is cheap enough.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Apply convexity discipline: seek cheap long-dated optionality with an identifiable explosive upside path.
insights.quote: inexpensive long-dated call options on things that could go explosively right
